description: Research (report only, no code): Jake saw a product called 'UB' (his spoken word; maybe UMI or similar), described as an open platform for large-scale robotics data collection. Identify the exact platform. Then go through its different gripper designs and report (1) which grippers have the most collected data (episodes, hours, tasks), and (2) which are the smallest and most compact (dimensions, weight). Give a ranked table for each, with sources, and note which fit Helping Hands (Aero Hand, VLA / MolmoAct2 zero-shot manipulation direction). Jake (voice, 2026-10-21): 'a product called UB, an open platform for large-scale robotics collection… go through the different gripper designs and see which ones have the most data, and which ones are the smallest or most compact.'

results.identified_issue: The first pass relied on the YUBI paper (8,434 h) and the Arena page (≈580 h), and its newest other source was FastUMI-100K (Oct 2025). The second pass found five gated HF parts, airoa-org/yubi-corl2026-umi-arena-01..05, totalling 17,853.7 h. I summed the 30 Hz durations from each card, and they do not include the separate 579.9 h initial repo (it may overlap). The card terms limit use to the competition. TacUMI's 30k h covers 6 embodiments, and the cards don't say how much is UMI. DataClaw's size and weight come from a retailer (aifitlab). The GenRobot license is unchecked. The Tencent card says 'fingertip UMI' but gives no device size. I used Awesome-UMI (chang-xinhai) as the index of new releases and spot-checked its key entries against the arXiv and HF pages.
results.summary: You were right: my first pass stopped at Oct 2025. YUBI's full set is now ≈17,850 h, and four more 1,000–5,000 h sets came out from August to October 2026.
results.detailed_description:
You were right. My first pass relied on the YUBI paper (June 2026) and topped out at FastUMI-100K from Oct 2025, so it missed everything from August to October. I re-ran the search against the Awesome-UMI index and checked the key entries against their Hugging Face cards and arXiv pages.

The biggest change is YUBI itself. AIRoA has now posted its full corpus on Hugging Face in five parts (6,588 + 2,075 + 2,013 + 3,935 + 3,242 h). That is ≈17,850 h and ≈8.9M episodes, double the paper's 8,434 h. It is still limited to UMI Arena teams, for competition use only.

New ranking by data collected:
1. NeoteAI TacUMI: 30k+ h (5,000 h open, NC)
2. YUBI: ≈17,850 h (gated)
3. GenRobot RealOmni: 10k h
4. Daimon DataClaw: 10k h (1,000 h open, NC, Oct 14)
5. Tencent fingertip UMI: 10k h (2,163 h open, CC BY)
6. RDT2: 10k h
7. HiFi-UMI: 6k h (2,000 h open, CC BY)

For size, YUBI's Glove is still the smallest at ≈319 g. The new runner-up is Daimon DataClaw at ≈388 g, 215 × 124 × 172 mm (retailer figures).

The new hardware with no big dataset yet is PolyUMI, KIWI, UMI ver.2 and iPhUMI. The YUBI hardware repo's last update was Sep 21, a ver2 refresh plus robot flanges; there is no ver3.

For Helping Hands, the largest data we can actually download is OpenNeoData (5k h, tactile, non-commercial). Tencent's and HiFi-UMI's ≈4,160 h together are the biggest commercially usable sets. The full tables are in plans/yubi_gripper_comparison.md.

results.notes: It looks like the latest one you got is from a year ago. I'm sure there have been more releases since then.

results.identified_issue: Mapped 'UB' to YUBI from the phonetics plus 'open platform … large-scale' (AIRoA's own framing). If Jake meant something else, the UMI-family tables still stand. Bounding boxes come from OCCT on the yubi-hw main-branch STEP files (SolidWorks export). The Glove ver2 bbox includes the Quest Touch Plus model; opt1/opt2 omit it. Masses are paper/retailer figures, not measured. FastUMI Pro/Go specs come from a retailer (aifitlab), which is a secondary source. RDT2's 10k h full-corpus release and its license are unverified, as are the HiFi-UMI and XRZero-G0 licenses. No CAD was changed, so there were no mating checks; I did not check a Mount 1 tool plate for the YUBI gripper.
results.summary: "UB" is YUBI, from Toyota and AIRoA. Its glove is the smallest handheld gripper (≈319 g) and ranks second for data (8,434 h).
results.detailed_description:
"UB" is almost certainly YUBI (Yielding Universal Bidigital Interface, arXiv 2606.10244, yubi.airoa.io), from Toyota's Frontier Research Center and AIRoA. They release the gripper hardware (CERN-OHL-W), software (Apache-2.0) and an 8,434 h dataset as one stack, and they run the CoRL 2026 UMI Arena around it.

YUBI itself publishes one design with variants: the Glove ver2 (the handheld collector; opt1/opt2 swap the finger attachment and pads) and a robot-side Gripper ver2 driven by a Dynamixel XM430, with flanges for UR5e, Franka, OpenArm and G1. I measured the published STEP assemblies with OCCT. The Glove is 105 × 188 × 198 mm with the Quest controller (105 × 167 × 198 mm without it). The robot gripper is 92 × 117 × 150 mm. All 8,434 h (1.20M episodes, 119 tasks) come from the Glove.

Since YUBI has only one design, I ranked it against the rest of the UMI family.
Most data: RDT2's rebuilt UMI ≈10,000 h (I could not confirm the full corpus is public) > YUBI 8,434 h > HiFi-UMI 2,000 h (public on HF) ≈ XRZero-G0 2,000 h > FastUMI-100K ≈600 h > PrimeBot UMI ≈205 h > original UMI ≈12 h.
Smallest: YUBI Glove ≈319 g > FastUMI Pro ≈600 g (270 × 162 × 215 mm) > UMI ≈780 g > FastUMI Go ≤800 g. The others publish no size.

For Helping Hands: YUBI's thumb-vs-index+middle jaws are the closest match to the Aero Hand's pinch, and the Glove is about the Aero Hand's length and weight. RDT2 is the one that shows zero-shot cross-embodiment, which is the MolmoAct2 direction. YUBI's data is non-commercial and gated: only ≈580 h is out, to UMI Arena teams, and policy submissions close Nov 2. HiFi-UMI-2K is the biggest fully public set. Full tables with sources are in plans/yubi_gripper_comparison.md.
